of evidence : 05.06.2018
Date of closing evidence : 06.08.2025
Opinion of the Judge : Accused found guilty
Offence complained : U/Sec.138 of Negotiable
Instrument Act.
Opinion of the Judge : Accused found guilty
3 C.C..16046/2018
JUDGMENT
This case is registered against the accused for the offence punishable U/s 138 of Negotiable
Instruments Act.
2. Factual matrix of the complainant's case is as under:
It is stated that the accused is the owner of the property bearing site No.187, 1st
Stage, formed in Sy.No.17, situated at Sonnenahalli Village, kengeri Hobli within the
limits of Sulikere Gramapanchayath, Bangalore South Taluk, measuring East to West
30 feet and North to South 20 feet along with building constructed in ground floor,
1st floor and 2nd floor, the accused has acquired the said property through a
Registered Sale Deed dated 26.10.2017. The accused has offered to sell the said
property and the offer was accepted by the complainant and accordingly on
07.05.2014 the complainant and the accused are entered into an agreement of sale in
respect of the said property, total sale consideration was fixed at Rs.11,00,000/-.
Accordingly, the complainant has paid a sum of Rs.10,00,000/- through cheque
bearing No.413896 drawn on COSMOS Bank, Basavanagudi Branch, Bengaluru to
the accused and the accused assured that there is no encumbrance on the said
property. The balance consideration amount of Rs.1,00,000/- is to be paid to the
accused at the time of registration of the sale deed. But accused unable to comply
with the terms and conditions of the agreement of sale and the accused requested the
complainant to enter into fresh agreement of sale. Accordingly, on 09.10.2015 the
complainant entered into an agreement of sale with the accused. As per the
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

agreement of sale dated 09.10.2015, the total sale consideration amount was
enhanced to Rs.36,00,000/-
and the complainant has paid Rs.20,00,000/- in following manner:
a) Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cheque bearing No.329275, drawn on Tumkur Grain
Merchant Co-operative Bank Ltd.
b) Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cash.
The complainant has paid total sum of Rs.30,00,000/- to the accused towards part sale
consideration amount in pursuance of the agreement of sale dated 07.05.2014 and 09.10.2015. As
per the agreement of sale the accused has required to execute and register the sale deed in favour of
the complainant within 12 months. But accused postponing in executing the registered sale deed. On
repeated requests made by the complainant, towards refund of advance sale consideration, the
accused has issued 2 cheques bearing No.465282 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.30,00,000/- and cheque
bearing No.465283 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.15,86,000/-, drawn on Sri Sudha Co- operative Bank
Ltd., Kengeri Branch, Bengaluru. The complainant presented the cheques before the bank, they got
dishonoured for the reason 'funds insufficient' vide memos dated 07.04.2018. Therefore, the
complainant got issued legal notice on 20.04.2018 demanding the accused to make payment
amount within 15 days and it was returned with a shara 'door locked, hence returned to the sender'.
However, the accused has not paid the cheques amount. Hence the complainant has constrained to
file the present complaint.
3. After receiving the complaint, this court has meticulously gone through the documents and
affidavit filed along with it and then took cognizance of the offence punishable U/sec.138 of
Negotiable Instruments Act and ordered for registration of the compliant as P.C.R.
4. Sworn statement of the complainant was recorded and marked 19 documents as Ex.P-1 to P-19.
As there were sufficient materials to constitute the offence, this court has proceeded to pass an order
for issuing process against the accused.
5. In pursuance of summons, accused has appeared through his counsel and applied for bail. He was
enlarged on bail. Then the substance of accusation was read over to the accused in the language
known to him, for which he pleaded not guilty.
6. As per the direction of Hon'ble supreme court in "Indian Bank Association V/s Union of India and
others reported in (2014)(5) SCC 590, this court treated the sworn statement of the complainant as
complainant evidence and posted matter for cross-examination of PW.1. The counsel for the accused
has fully cross- examined PW.1. Thereafter the complainant closed his side of evidence.
7. The statement of accused as contemplated under the provisions of Section 313 of Cr.P.C has been
recorded vide order dated 06.11.2023 and the incriminating evidence as such forthcoming against
the accused in the evidence of PW.1 and the documents has been read over and explained to the
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

accused in the language known to him. He denied all incriminating evidence.
8. In order to substantiate his defense, the accused got himself examined orally as DW.1 and got
marked Ex.D1 to 6. DW.1 has been cross-examined by the learned counsel for the complainant.
9. I have heard the arguments of the learned counsel for both the side. The learned counsel for
complainant filed written arguments. Learned Counsel for both side also filed memo with citations.
I have perused the oral and the documentary evidence placed on record and gone through those case
laws.
10. Points that arise for my consideration are as under:
1. Whether the complainant proves that the accused towards discharge of his liability
issued 2 cheques bearing No.465282 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.30,00,000/- and
cheque bearing No.465283 dated 06.04.2018 for Rs.15,86,000/-, drawn on
Sri.Sudha Co-
opearative Bank Ltd., Kengeri Branch, Bangalore in favour of complainant, on presentation of the
same for encashment, they were dishonored for "Funds Insufficient" in the account maintained by
the accused, then in-spite of issuing demand notice to the Accused and in complying with statutory
requirement under Negotiable Instrument Act, Accused did not repay the cheques amount, thereby
he has committed an offence punishable U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act?
2. What Order?
11. My Answer to above points are as under:-
Point No.I :- In the Affirmative,
Point No.II :- As per the final order for
the following....
REASONS
12. POINT NO.I:- The Defense of the accused that:
He has borrowed Rs.10 lakhs from the complainant through one Mr.Muniyappa, who
is manager of Sudha Co- operative Bank. While taking the loan the complainant has
put condition to repay the said loan by way of cash and for security purpose he has
taken blank e-stamp papers, 10 to 15 blank bond papers and 2 signed cheques and his
property documents. He has repaid said loan with interest to the complainant.
Thereafter, he requested the complainant to return back his security cheques, but the
complainant insisted for higher rate of interest. That time he met Mr.Muniyappa and
told him about the same, Mr.Muniyappa assured to get back the documents from the
complainant, but in meanwhile Mr.Muniyappa has been murdered and the wife of
the Mr.Muniyappa has given complaint against the complainant alleging that he has
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

murdered him.
13. He has lodged a police compliant against accused. The complainant has misused his security
cheques and filed this case. He has not filled the details in the cheques. The complainant has filed
several cheque bounce cases against different persons. Hence, on these grounds, accused prays to
acquit him from this case.
14. Advocate for accused has relied on the citations reported CDJ 2024 All HC 180 in between
Archana Singh Gautam V/s State of U.P and another, CDJ 2024 APHC 1172 in between Ganta
Kavitha Devi V/s The State of Andhra Pradesh, CDJ 2006 SC 492 in between M.S.Narayana Memon
@ Mani V/s State of Kerala & Another, CDJ 2001 SC1423 in between Sasseriyil Joseph V/s
Devassia, CDJ 2019 SC 471 in between Basalingappa V/s Mudibasappa, CDJ 2018 MHC 7496 in
between Mohan V/s S.Nagarajan, CDJ 2018 APHC 970 in between V.Naga Vinay V/s Ch.Sambasiva
Rao and another, CDJ 2015 MHC 8046 in between S.Balamani V/s Vijayashanthi, CDJ 2024 SC 665
in between Sri Dattatraya V/s Sharanappa, Crl.A.No.533/2015 in between H.V.Jagannatha V/s
Prabhakar B.J, I have gone through those case laws.
15. Negotiable Instruments Act provides for some presumption in favour of the complainant i.e.,
Section 118 reads as here: - "That every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration
and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was
accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration".
16. Further Sec 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides for presumption in favour of a
holder. It reads as here: - "It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a
cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in sec 138, for the discharge, in whole or in
part, or any debt or other liability."
17. Combined reading of above said sections raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the
cheque that he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability.
However, it is settled principle of law that the presumption available u/s 139 NI Act can be rebutted
by the accused by raising a probable defense.
18. The complainant has examined as PW.1 and he has reiterated the contents of complaint in his
chief- examination. He has got marked Ex.P1 to P19. He has produced the cheques issued by
accused and the same is marked as Ex.P-1 & 2, the signature of the accused is marked as Ex.P-1(a) &
2(a), copies of bank memos are marked as Ex.P-3 & P-4, copy of demand notice dated:20.04.2018 is
marked as Ex.P-5, copy of postal receipt is marked as Ex.P-6, copy of returned notice is marked as
Ex.P-7, postal cover is marked as Ex.P-8, postal receipt is marked as Ex.P-9, copy of postal
acknowledgment is marked as Ex.P-10, copy of absolute sale deed is marked as Ex.P-11, copies of
agreement of sale are marked as Ex.P-12 & P-13, Ex.P-14 & P-15 are the bank statements, bank
memos are marked as Ex.P-16 & P17, copy of statement of account is marked as Ex.P-18 and copy of
letter addressed to the bank is marked as Ex.P-19. He has been cross-examined by the counsel for
the accused.
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

19. Percontra, the accused has also stepped into witness box and orally deposed about his defense as
stated supra and he has been cross-examined by the counsel for the complainant.
20. Advocate for complainant has relied on the citations reported (2015) 8 SCC 378 in between
T.Vasanthakumar V/s Vijayakumari, (2010) 11 SCC 441 in between Rangappa V/s Sri Mohan and
(2007) 6 SCC 555 in between C.C.Alavi Haji V/s Palapetty Muhammed and another, I have gone
through those case laws.
21. I have heard orally both side counsel and perused the written arguments filed by both side.
Having regard to the pleadings and evidence placed on record it appears that acquaintance between
the parties is not in dispute. At the outset the accused has admitted that both cheques at Ex.P1 and
P2 belong to his account and he has duly signed on those cheques. Therefore, it is proved that
cheques belongs to the account of the accused and they are issued in the name of the complainant.
22. Therefore, initial presumption U/Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act has to be drawn in favour of the
complainant as the Honorable Supreme Court of India in "Triyambak S Hegde v Sripad" (2022) 1
SCC 742 while relying upon the the constitution bench judgment of Basalingappa v Mudibasappa
(2019) 5 SCC 418, under para 14 of its judgment reiterated that "once the cheque was issued and
that the signatures are upon the cheque are accepted by the accused, the presumptions undee Sec
118 and 139 of the NI Act arise against the accused. That is, unless the contrary is proved, it shall be
presumed that the cheques in question were drawn by the accused for a consideration and that the
complainant had received the cheque in question in discharge of debt/liability from the accused."
23. Therefore, as per Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act initial presumption has to drawn infavour of the
complainant that cheque is issued in discharge of legally enforceable debt. The burden lies on the
accused to rebut the said initial presumption on the scale of preponderance of probabilities.
24. In nutshell case of the complainant is that the accused has agreed to sell his property for total
sale consideration of Rs.36,00,000/- and received Rs.30,00,000/- as advance consideration and
executed sale agreements dated 07.05.2014 and 09.10.2015. But he failed to execute the sale deed
and finally to refund the advance amount the accused has agreed to give Rs.45,86,000/- and issued
cheques in discharge of the said liability, but those cheques dishonoured for the reason 'funds
insufficient'. Hence this case.
24. Even in his evidence, the complainant has reiterated the averments of the complaint. Though the
counsel for the accused has much cross-examined PW.1 regarding his source of income, his
occupation, his ITR documents, his land details and tried to dispute the financial capacity of PW.1, it
is worth mentioning here that in the chief-examination of accused, he himself has admitted that
through one Mr.Muniyappa, he met the complainant and borrowed Rs.10,00,000/- loan from
complainant.
25. Therefore, the series of questions asked by the counsel for the accused regarding financial
capacity of the complainant holds no water, as accused himself has admitted the financial
transaction with the complainant. However, as per the complainant, he has paid Rs.30,00,000/-
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

towards advance sale consideration vide agreement of sale dated 07.05.2014 and 09.10.2015.
26. Percontra, the accused contends that he never intended to sell his property, but he borrowed
loan of Rs 10 lakhs from the complainant to which his signatures were taken in a blank stamp
papers and bond papers for security purpose.
27. Firstly, the complainant has produced original sale deed dated 26.10.2007 at Ex.P11 which
shows that title of the accused pertaining to the property intended to be sell. Ex.P12 is the sale
agreement dated 07.05.2014, Ex.P-13 is the sale agreement dated 09.10.2015 executed by the
accused in favour of the complainant. The accused admits his signature on Ex.P12 &P13 sale
agreements, but he deposed in his cross-examination that his signature was taken in a blank sheets.
It is pertinent to note here that the accused is the pygmy collector by profession, he deposed in his
cross examination that he has complete knowledge about banking transaction. When such being the
case, he being a prudent person of having worldly knowledge, this statement of the accused that he
has singed to a blank e-stamp papers and bond papers, cheques appears to be vague and does not
transpires the confidence of the Court. Nothing worth is elicited from the mouth of PW.1 to prove
that he had taken blank e- stamp papers and bond papers, signed cheques from the accused for
security purpose. Mere making suggestions to witness is not suffice. Therefore, there is no reason to
suspect Ex.P12 & 13 sale agreements executed by the accused in favour of the complainant.
28. On perusal of recitals of Ex.P12, at page No.2, it is crystal clear that accused has unequivocally
admitted that he has received Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cheque and Rs.20,00,000/- by way of
cheques & cash as per Ex.P13. ExP14 and 15 are bank account statement of the complainant which
clearly shows that through cheque bearing No.413896 and 329275 Rs.20 lakhs has been transferred
to accused.
30. During cross-examination in para No.3, the accused has admitted that he has received
Rs.10,00,000/- by way of cheque from the complainant. Further he denied that as per Ex.P-13 he
increased the sale consideration from Rs.11 laks to Rs.25 lakhs, He pleaded ignorance to the
suggestion as per Ex.P15 and 14 account statement he received Rs.10 lakhs each. He denied the
suggestion totally he received Rs.20 lakhs by way of cheques and Rs.10 lakhs by way of cash.
31. If at all accused has not received 20 lakhs by way of cheque, he ought to have produced his
account statements before the court to show his bonafide. He has produced only complaints filed by
complainant against others. But not produced any admissible evidence to believe that he has not
received amount of RS 20 lakhs by way cheques from the complainant.
32. In AIR 2023 SC 5018 in between Rajesh Jain V/s Ajay Singh, Apex court held that " 31.
Presumption, on the other hand, literally means "taking as true without examination or proof". In
Kumar Exports v. Sharma Exports, this Court referred to presumption as "devices by use of which
courts are enabled and entitled to pronounce on an issue notwithstanding that there is no evidence
or insufficient evidence."
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

33. As per above case law and in view of strong legal presumption given U/Sec.118 and 139 of NI Act
the oral evidence of PW.1 corroborated with the documentary evidence at Ex.P12 & 13 I.e. sale
agreements, and Exp14 and 15 account statements, the complainant has proved that he has paid
Rs.30,00,000/- to the accused. Moreover, the accused has expressly admitted the financial capacity
of PW.1 to advance a sum of Rs 10,00,000/-. In light of such admission, it is not open to the accused
to dispute the financial capacity of PW.1 with respect to the remaining sum of Rs.20,00,000/-, as
such, such contention is inconsistent and untenable.
34. Sanjabij Tari vs Kishore S.Borcar, 2025 SCC Online SC 2069 Apex court held that "20. However,
this Court is of the view that any breach of Section 269SS of the IT Act, 1961 is subject to a penalty
only under Section 271D of the IT Act, 1961. Further neither Section 269SS nor 271D of the IT Act,
1961 state that any transaction in breach thereof will be illegal, invalid or statutorily void. Therefore,
any violation of Section 269SS would not render the transaction unenforceable under Section 138 of
the NI Act or rebut the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act because such a
person, assuming him/her to be the payee/holder in due course, is liable to be visited by a penalty
only as prescribed. Consequently, the view that any transaction above Rs.20,000/- (Rupees Twenty
Thousand) is illegal and void and therefore does not fall within the definition of 'legally enforceable
debt' cannot be countenanced. Accordingly, the conclusion of law in P.C. Hari (supra) is set aside. '
34. Thus as per above case law, cash transaction is perse not illegal.
35. The only defense taken by the accused is that he has repaid entire loan to the complainant with
interest. He disputes the extent of amount received. But irrespective of whether the amount in
question is construed as refund of advance sale consideration or as repayment of a loan, the accused
is legally bound to repay the sum received from the complainant. Although the accused has disputed
the nature of the transaction, such dispute does not absolve him of his liability to return the
admitted amount.
36. In the cross-examination at para No.10 the accused has deposed that for Rs.30,00,000/-, he has
paid 10% interest and it comes to Rs.3,00,000/-. He could not depose on which dates he has paid
interest and principal amount to the complainant. But he told that he has paid it in presence of one
Mr.Muniyappa. He deposed that he does not know exactly how much he has repaid so far to the
complainant, but he has paid it in 2016-17 itself.
37. Therefore, except his self interested testimony, the accused has not produced any admissible
evidence before the Court to prove that he has repaid principal with interest to the complainant. The
accused has contended that at the request of the complainant, he has repaid the entire amount by
way of cash and same appears to be vague, untenable and does not transpires the confidence of the
Court. Admittedly, the accused is doing pigmy collection work having sufficient worldly knowledge
about the loan transaction, banking transaction and also has complete knowledge about the
potential consequences of issuance of blank signed stamp papers or bond papers and cheques.
When such being the case, despite of having knowledge of issuance of blank signed cheques to the
complainant, the accused contends that he has repaid entire interest and principal amount by way of
cash without keeping any proof for payment appears highly improbable and raises serious suspicion.
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

38. No prudent person would pay entire amount by way of cash without keeping any
acknowledgment for having paid such huge amount. Admittedly Mr.Muniyappa is no more. Counsel
for the accused has argued that in said murder case, complainant was one of the accused persons
and he got enlarged on bail. Percontra, counsel for the complainant has argued that in the said case,
some other persons have been convicted with life imprisonment and it is not related to the accused.
However, both have not substantiated their arguments with cogent evidence. The questions as to
whether Mr. Muniyappa died a natural death or was murdered, and if so, by whom, are wholly
irrelevant to the dispute involved in the present case.
39. Even otherwise, the alleged involvement of the complainant in the said murder case, whether
established or not, does not absolve the accused of his burden to prove the defence that he has
repaid the entire amount to the complainant. Court cannot travel beyond the scope of this case. The
accused must independently discharge the burden of proving repayment, and cannot rely on
unrelated allegations to evade liability of cheques.
40. No documentary evidence is produced to prove that the accused was possessing such amount to
repay the same to the complainant at relevant point of time. Thus contention of repayment, lacks
corroboration. In the cross-examination he has stated that he has repaid entire amount in 2016-17
itself. If that was the case, accused ought to have immediately taken steps to recover back the alleged
security documents and cheques from the complainant. No such endeavor is made by the accused
for the reasons best known to him.
41. He has deposed in his cross-examination that the complainant has refused to return back his
security documents and claimed higher rate of interest, subsequently he informed the same to
Mr.Muniyappa also. Therefore, as per his own version in early 2017 itself the complainant become
hostile to return back the security documents to him. Under such circumstances, any prudent
person would have taken legal action against the complainant in anticipating of misuse of the
documents or the cheques. He deposed that he has lodged a police complaint before CCB and he has
given statement before the police. He has also deposed that police have told him that one
Mr.Ravindra has already lodged complaint as per Ex. D6 and he can give statement in the said case.
42. Though DW1 couldn't identify his statement at ExD6 during cross examination, even such
statement is given also, same will not exonerate the accused from repaying the amount to the
complainant. If he is charging exorbitant interest, complainant shall face legal consequence as pe
ExD6 and same is not a ground discharge the accused from this case.
43. Admittedly both cheques are dishonoured for the reason 'funds insufficient'. Being vigilant
person, accused could have given 'stop payment instructions' to his banker, even such efforts is also
not made by the accused for the reasons best known to him. After cheques got dishonoured the
complainant has issued legal notice as per Ex.P7 and same is returned with a shara 'door lock'.
Though accused has contended that notice is not served on him, he has not disputed the address
shown in the legal notice.
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

44. Apex court in MMTC Ltd. and Another vs. Medchl Chemicals & Pharma (P) Ltd. and Another,
(2002) 1 SCC 234 has specifically held that when a statutory notice is not replied, it has to be
presumed that the cheque was issued towards the discharge of liability.
45. It is held in 2006 CRI.L.J.1, in a case of Gorantala Venkateswara Rao. V/s. Kolla Veera Raghava
Rao and another, that;
"(B) Negotiable Instrument Act ( 26 of 1881), S.138 -
Dishonour of cheque- Legally enforceable debt- Failure of accused in giving reply to legal notice
issued by complainant- Is one of the strong circumstances to draw inference that accused borrowed
amount from complainant and cheque was issued towards part payment of legally enforceable debt."
46. In C.C. Alavi Haji vs Palapetty Muhammed & Anr (2007) 6 SCC 555, the Hon'ble Apex court has
held; "
17. It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear
departure from the rule of Criminal Law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a
notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the
notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in
respect of the complaint under Sec 138 the Act, make payment of the cheque amount
and submit to the Court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of
summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the
complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt
of the summons from the Court along with the copy of the complaint under Sec 138 of
the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as under
Sec 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Sec 27 of the G.C.
Act and Sec 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the
proviso would defeat the very object of the legislation... "
47. Therefore, defense of the accused that notice is not served holds no water as he has not deposited
cheques amount before court as per law laid down by Apex court in aforementioned case law. The
accused has not given reply to the notice and same is fatal to his defense. Therefore, it is evident that
except oral say of accused, no credible, cogent, admissible evidence brought before the court to
prove his defense that he has repaid entire amount to the complainant.
48. It is observed by the Court that for every question posed, the accused has given vague answers,
stating that he was relying on Mr. Muniyappa and the repayment of the amount was made through
him etc. It is further contended that Mr. Muniyappa had assured him that the documents would be
retrieved from the complainant. However, However, in view of the fact that Mr. Muniyappa is no
more, the possibility that the accused has taken such a stand only to avoid liability arising out of the
cheques cannot be ruled out and it appears to be clear after thought.
Anekal Krishnappa vs Srinivasa on 22 April, 2026

49. Though counsel for the accused has contended that there is no seal and signatures of the bank,
on bank memos Ex.P3 & P4, by producing Ex.P16 and P17 bank memos as well as his account
statement at Ex.P18, the complainant has clearly demonstrated that he has presented both the
cheques to the bank and same is suffice to hold that the complainant has presented both the cheques
to the bank.
50. In most recent case regarding Sec 146 of NI Act, , Jagdish R vs Sri B S Ravi CRL.RP No. 1081 of
2018, Decided on 16 April, 2026, Hon'ble karanataka High court, held that "26. Therefore, the first
contention on which the learned counsel for the revision petitioner has stated that there could not
be any criminal prosecution for dishonor of the cheque, inasmuch as the bank memo did not contain
proper endorsement of dishnour cannot be countenanced in law. Likewise, the contention that the
seal and signature of the bank was a mandatory requirement when the cheque was sent for manual
collection cannot also be accepted.
27. In view of the electronic clearance, the seal and signature is not mandatory and therefore, seal
and signature, official mark etc., on Ex.P.2 cannot be a ground to reject the complaint.
28. Since the complainant enjoys the presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments
Act, 1881, if at all the accused is of the opinion that bank endorsement vide Exhibit P-2 is
incomplete or incorrect, he could have summoned his banker to establish that he had sufficient
money in his account and the cheque was not presented to his banker at all for collection.
29. Therefore, the ground that in view of Section 146 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881,
complaint is not maintainable, cannot also be countenanced in law. "
51. As per above case law, merely because the seal and signatures are not appearing
in the bank memos, which are produced initially, the entire case of the complainant
cannot be brushed aside.
52. The counsel for the accused has argued that after lapse of 3 years, from the date of
sale agreement, the complaint is filed, this compliant, as it is not maintainable which
is pertaining to time barred debt or liability and also relied upon the citations. I have
gone through those case laws. It is significant to note here that as per the sale
agreement, the accused has agreed to execute the sale deed within 12 months from
the date of agreement of sale, which comes to an end on 09.10.2018. The complaint is
filed on 05.06.2018. There is an initial presumption regarding date of issuance of the
cheques as per Sec.118 of NI Act. Accordingly, Ex.P1 cheques have been issued on
06.04.2018. It is not proved that the cheques were issued in 2015 as alleged by the
accused. Therefore issuance of cheques revives transaction in question, as such it is
not construed as time barred debt or liability. Even otherwise within 2 years from the
date of second agreement the complaint is filed.
53. In M/S M K Enterprises vs Kumari Varsha Pole, on 17 December, 2021
CRIMINAL REVISION PETITION NO. 375/20 Hon'ble Karnataka High Court, held

39. Thus, when the questions formulated by the learned Single Judge of High Court

the creditor might have enforced payment, but for the law for the limitation of suits
and as such, the cheque becomes a cheque drawn towards discharge of a legally
enforceable debt as contemplated by the explanation to Section 138 of the NI Act.

40. In view of the settled position of law, even if the contention of the learned counsel
for the petitioner that the cheques were issued towards a time barred debt is to be
accepted, by applying the above principle of law to the present case, issuance of
cheques in question amount to written promise to pay the said debt, as provided

57. Further accused contends that complainant has filed various cheque bounce cases
against different persons and also produced copies of those complaints before the
Court and contends that he is money lender. Merely filing of multiple cheque bounce

58. Sec 24 of The Karnataka Money-Lenders Act, 1961, says that regarding Procedure
of court in suits regarding loans.--
'(b) if the Court finds that the provisions of section 20 or section 21 have not been
complied with by the money- lender, it may, if the plaintiff's claim is established, in
whole or in part, disallow the whole or any portion of the interest found due as may
seem reasonable to it in the circumstances of the case and may disallow costs.'
59. As per the said Act and the Rules framed thereunder, a money-lender is required
to submit a report in the prescribed format to the prescribed authority. Non-
compliance with this requirement constitutes a violation of the said provisions.
However, such non-compliance does not, in any manner, affect the maintainability of
a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
60. By virtue of Section 24 of the Act, if the civil court finds that the provisions of
Sections 20 and 21 have not been complied with by the money-lender, the court may
disallow the whole or any portion of the interest found due. It is for the competent
authority under the Act to initiate appropriate action against a money-lender who has

habitual money-lender is not sustainable in law.

64. ((2019) 4 SCC 197) ie Bir Singh V Mukesh Kumar, Apex court has held that "A meaningful

for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. It is immaterial that the cheque may have been
filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If the
cheque is otherwise valid, the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted".

signing of the cheque cannot be rebutted merely by the report of a hand-writing expert. Even if the
details in the cheque have not been filled up by drawer but by another person, this is not relevant to
the defense whether cheque was issued towards payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. '
66. Thus, in light of Section 20 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and the above-cited case laws, any
inconsistencies in handwriting, pen, or ink on the cheques do not absolve the accused of liability,
particularly when he has admitted the issuance of the cheques in favour of the complainant.

failed to rebut the initial presumption given in favour of the complainant. Nothing worth is elicited
from the mouth of PW.1 to suspect his case. Indeed by produced required amount of oral and
documentary evidence, the complainant has proved his case beyond reasonable doubts. Further this
court makes it clear that it cannot consider the some facts urged by the accused which are
completely out of the scope of this summary proceeding case. With these observations court proceed
